lessons.title: The browser asks, the server answers
lessons.blurb: Your page is the client. It sends a request to a server and waits for a response. In JavaScript, fetch(url) sends the request, and every response comes back with a status code that says how it went.
notes: The server lives at `https://bakery.flowpad.test`. The menu is at the path `/menu`.
`const res = await fetch(url)` waits for the response. `await` only works inside an `async function`.
`res.status` is a number: `200` means OK. Watch the network panel below as you type.

lessons.title: Responses carry data
lessons.blurb: A status code alone says little. The body of the response carries the data, and APIs usually send it as JSON: text that looks like JavaScript objects and arrays. Turn it into real objects with res.json().
notes: `const items = await res.json()` gives you an array of menu items.
Each item looks like `{ id, name, type, price }`. Open a row in the network panel to see the raw JSON.
Build the list with a loop, e.g. `for (const item of items) { ... }`.

lessons.title: Ask for exactly what you need
lessons.blurb: The URL can carry questions. A query string starts with ? and holds name=value pairs. Instead of downloading everything and filtering in the browser, you can ask the server to do the filtering.
notes: This server understands `type`. Try `/menu?type=pastry` and look at the response.
Several pairs are joined with `&`, like `?a=1&b=2`.

lessons.title: When the answer is no
lessons.blurb: Not every request succeeds. The server says why with the status code: 4xx means the client asked for something wrong, 5xx means the server failed. fetch does not throw on a 404, so your code has to check.
notes: `/menu/1` returns one item. There is no item `42`, so `/menu/42` returns `404`.
`res.ok` is `true` for any 2xx status and `false` otherwise.
The body of an error response often explains the problem. Open the row to read it.

lessons.title: Sending data to the server
lessons.blurb: GET reads. POST sends data that asks the server to create something. The data travels in the request body, usually as JSON, and a header tells the server what kind of data it is.
notes: `fetch(url, { method: "POST", headers: {...}, body: ... })` — the second argument describes the request.
The body must be text: `JSON.stringify({ item_id: 3, quantity: 2 })`. Add the header `"Content-Type": "application/json"`.
A new order comes back as `201 Created` with an `order_id`. A `400` means the body was wrong; read its message.

lessons.title: Order, then follow up
lessons.blurb: Real apps chain requests: the answer to one becomes part of the next. Create an order, take the order_id from the response, and use it to ask the server where your order is.
notes: Resources have addresses: an order lives at `/orders/<order_id>`.
Build the path from data: `"https://bakery.flowpad.test/orders/" + created.order_id`.
Each request is separate — the server only knows the order because you sent its id.
